strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation: The distinction between planning-level and grounding-level domain bias is clear and intuitive, addressing a genuine gap in GUI agent capabilities.

Clever subtitle-driven retrieval design: The three-stage retrieval pipeline (domain classification → topic extraction → relevance matching) is more sophisticated than keyword matching. Achieves high precision (100%) and recall (91%) on domain classification with human evaluation support.

Comprehensive experimental validation: Evaluation across three agent architectures (Seed-1.8, Qwen3-VL-8B, AgentS3) with detailed ablations on element count, annotation models, and per-domain analysis. Results demonstrate consistency.

Plug-and-play integration: Framework requires no model fine-tuning or architectural changes, making it practically deployable to different agents. Shows graceful degradation when knowledge is unavailable.

Systematic cost analysis: Detailed breakdown showing $114.6 total cost for full benchmark with practical comparison to manual annotation. Different annotators tested showing robustness to model choice.
Honest failure analysis: Section F and appendices provide concrete failure examples revealing limitations (planning mismatches, grounding mismatches) rather than hiding them.
Clean knowledge decomposition: Separating planning and grounding knowledge targeting distinct agent components is conceptually sound.
weaknesses: Significant retrieval coverage gap: Only 82.8% (299/361) tasks retrieve relevant videos. The remaining 17.2% degrade to baseline performance. No analysis of why certain tasks fail or strategies to improve coverage for cross-application workflows.

Grounding knowledge provides minimal value: Accounts for only 0.69-0.80% additional improvement over planning alone. On some domains (Impress, VSCode), grounding hurts performance. This substantially undermines one of the paper's two claimed innovations.

Modest overall improvements: 4.5-7.5% gains on strong baselines (AgentS3 at 50.18%→54.65%) are consistent but incremental. Planning dominates with 85-91% of gains, suggesting the approach is primarily a better prompting mechanism.

Critical dependence on retrieval quality: Failure cases (Fig. 7-8) show procedurally mismatched videos lead to dead ends or browser detours wasting many steps. No effective mitigation beyond suggesting 'stricter filtering.' The 'reference not directive' framing doesn't prevent agents from being misled.

Incomplete annotation quality evaluation: The 'Meaningful' filter achieves only 91.6% precision and 53.6% recall on idle no-action frames (Appendix D). Human evaluation only covers retrieval stages (Fig. 5), not downstream planning/grounding quality or VLM hallucinations in annotation.

Narrow evaluation scope: Only OSWorld (desktop applications in controlled VMs) tested. No evaluation on mobile GUIs, web interfaces, or niche software. Generalization to scenarios with sparse YouTube tutorials unknown.

Weak inverse dynamics formulation: Equation (1) doesn't technically capture inverse dynamics. Output is natural language descriptions, not action parameters. The terminology is somewhat misleading about what the method actually does.

Confounding experimental factors: Annotation uses GPT-5.1 but execution uses different VLMs. Ablations on element count and annotation models use only 50-task subsets with high variance (Table 3). Per-domain results show inconsistency (OS: 1 task, ThBrd: 3 tasks) limiting statistical meaningfulness.

Insufficient baseline comparisons: Only Watch & Learn [22] directly compared (indirectly via different configs). RAGGUI, KG-RAG, OS-Symphony mentioned but not evaluated. Claims of 'substantially larger gains' rest on limited comparison data.

No discussion of inference latency: Per-step latency increases from 9.5→11.6s (+2.1s). Real-time YouTube search adds retrieval time not quantified. Total wall-clock overhead and feasibility for interactive scenarios unclear.

Incomplete design justifications: Default k=7 for grounding elements chosen arbitrarily; ablation shows k=5 is better. Dual-anchored relevance prompt (repeating topic three times) lacks ablation or justification. Subtitle truncation to 10K characters not justified.

Reproducibility limitations: Depends on proprietary APIs (GPT-5.1, GPT-4.1, Whisper). YouTube search stability not discussed. No code release mentioned. Whisper transcription errors could cascade through pipeline.
Statistical rigor: No confidence intervals, significance tests, or multiple runs reported. Some per-domain subsets very small (Table 3), making results potentially unreliable.

Innovative subtitle-driven Video-RAG pipeline achieving 77.33% direct-match retrieval accuracy, substantially outperforming title-only (67.67%) and random baselines (45.33%)

Comprehensive experimental validation across three architecturally different agents (Seed-1.8, Qwen3-VL-8B, AgentS3) with consistent improvements of +4.47–+7.48pp and successful cross-benchmark transfer to WindowsAgentArena without task-specific tuning
Extensive ablation studies (Tables 3–6) isolating contributions of planning (86–91% of gains) vs. grounding, number of retrieved videos (K=2 optimal), and annotation pipeline components

Training-free, architecture-agnostic framework requiring no model parameter modification, enabling seamless plug-and-play integration with diverse agent designs through natural language knowledge representation

weaknesses: Significant failure modes when retrieval quality degrades: procedurally mismatched videos cause planning knowledge to actively harm performance (8–50 steps wasted on dead ends); 17.2% of tasks retrieve no relevant videos and fall back silently to baseline

Modest improvements with substantial overhead: +4.47–+7.48pp gains combined with 22% per-step latency increase (9.5s→11.6s) and marginal step reduction (15.7 vs. 16.6); wall-clock time improvement unclear; grounding alone contributes only +0.41pp despite complex implementation

Limited technical novelty: subtitle-driven filtering is novel for video RAG but individual components are standard (LLM classification, VLM annotation, RAG integration); inverse-dynamics-style pairwise annotation is well-established; value lies in system integration rather than algorithmic innovation

Retrieval robustness concerns: 82.8% coverage (17.2% task failure), aggressive filtering funnel (50+ → ≤2 videos), YouTube availability/subtitle quality not guaranteed, no analysis of generalization to niche or specialized software

Experimental setup concerns: Seed-1.8 baseline requires 'lightweight parsing fixes' for malformed outputs (reproducibility risk); Chrome domain affected by network issues (evaluation cleanliness); Qwen3-VL baseline from external reference not re-implemented

Limited generalization scope: evaluation confined to Linux desktop (OSWorld) and Windows widgets (WAA); no evidence on mobile UIs, cloud-based platforms, or web-only applications despite mentioning these in related work

Incomplete comparative analysis: Watch & Learn appears only in Table 3, not direct comparison on same conditions; RAGGUI, KG-RAG, OS-Symphony mentioned in related work but not empirically compared; subtitle-only vs. full visual pipeline limited to 120-task subset (Table 4)

Insufficient understanding of design choices: why does grounding contribute so little (+0.41pp) despite complex annotation pipeline; non-monotonic gains with additional videos (Table 5) not fully investigated; no analysis of knowledge degradation across software versions or UI layout changes
